facts.statement: Indosinosuchus peninsularensis is classified as a member of the family Teleosauridae.
facts.quote: A member of the family Teleosauridae.

facts.statement: The type locality for Indosinosuchus peninsularensis is the Khlong Min Formation.
facts.quote: Type locality: Khlong Min Formation

facts.statement: Fossils of Indosinosuchus peninsularensis have been found in Thailand.
facts.quote: Country: Thailand

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus peninsularensis lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Age: Middle-Late Jurassic

facts.statement: While the genus Indosinosuchus is generally dated to the Middle to Late Jurassic, some studies suggest an Early Cretaceous age for the Phu Kradung Formation.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Middle Jurassic - Late Jurassic ~ Some studies have proposed an Early Cretaceous age for the Phu Kradung Formation

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus lived during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous in what is now Thailand.
facts.quote: Indosinosuchus is a genus of teleosaurid crocodyliform that lived during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous in what is now Thailand.

facts.statement: While the type species of Indosinosuchus is known from freshwater environments, I. peninsularensis is considered a marine species.
facts.quote: It is unique among teleosauroids as the type species is the only named genus known from a freshwater environment, while most other members including I. peninsularensis are marine.

facts.statement: Material for Indosinosuchus peninsularensis was collected from the Ban Nam Pun site in 2004.
facts.quote: Fossil discoveries attributed to Indosinosuchus date as far back as the mid to late 2000s, with material having been collected from the Ban Nam Pun site of Thailand's Khlong Min Formation in 2004

facts.statement: Remains of Indosinosuchus were found at the Phu Noi locality in 2008.
facts.quote: and other remains having been found in the sediments of the Phu Noi locality, part of the Phu Kradung Formation, in 2008.

facts.statement: By 2019, ten individuals of Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis were known from the Phu Kradung Formation.
facts.quote: By 2019, when Martin and colleagues named Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis, ten individuals known from skull remains and various assorted postcranial fossils were known from the Phu Kradung Formation, all collected from Phu Noi.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis has four teeth per premaxilla, 30 teeth per maxilla, and 31 teeth per dentary.
facts.quote: Four teeth are situated in each premaxilla of I. potamosiamensis, organized into two closely spaced pairs, followed by 30 teeth in either of the only faintly ornamented maxillae and opposed by 31 dentary teeth.

facts.statement: All teeth of Indosinosuchus are slender, conical, and have curved crowns.
facts.quote: All teeth are slender and conical in shape with a curved crown.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus has wider-than-long osteoderms in the trunk and longer-than-wide subrectangular osteoderms on the tail, all with a front-to-back keel.
facts.quote: The osteoderm armor of Indosinosuchus follows the patterns typical for teleosaurs, with wider than long osteoderms in the trunk region and longer than wide, subrectangular osteoderms on the tail, all of which preserve a keel that runs from the front to the back.

facts.statement: The precise age of Indosinosuchus is debated, with vertebrate fossils suggesting a Late Jurassic age and palynological data suggesting an Early Cretaceous age.
facts.quote: The precise age of Indosinosuchus is unclear, as the vertebrate fossils of the Phu Kradung Formation support a Late Jurassic age, while palynological data suggests an Early Cretaceous (Berriasian) age.

facts.statement: The validity of Indosinosuchus kalasinensis as a distinct species was questioned in a 2026 study by Lauprasert et al., who argued it was synonymous with I. potamosiamensis.
facts.quote: However, this conclusion was eventually questioned in a 2026 study by Komsorn Lauprasert and colleagues as they described the teleosauroid material from Ban Nam Pun.

facts.statement: In a 2019 study, Indosinosuchus was initially classified as a close relative or sister taxon of Machimosaurus hugii.
facts.quote: In the initial description by Martin and colleagues in 2019, Indosinosuchus was recovered as a close relative of the robust teleosauroid Machimosaurus hugii, with one analysis even recovering as sister taxa.

facts.statement: Later analyses separated Indosinosuchus and Machimosaurus into different families, teleosaurids and machimosaurids, respectively.
facts.quote: Unlike in Martin's previous study, Indosinosuchus was not found to clade anywhere near Machimosaurus, with the two genera falling into entirely different families, the teleosaurids and the machimosaurids.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the lack of preserved postcranial material for I. kalasinensis may explain why phylogenetic studies fail to recover a clear relationship between its species.
facts.quote: Part of the reason for this lack of a recovered relationship could be the lack of material for I. kalasinensis and the fact that the two species do not preserve as much of the postcranial skeleton as their relatives.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus evolved convergent adaptations with machimosaurids, including robust jaws and strong muscle attachments.
facts.quote: Their study revealed several key adaptations of Indosinosuchus that show that these teleosaurs at least partially evolved convergently to machimosaurids, possessing relatively robust jaws with strong muscle attachments.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis possessed a strong bite comparable to derived machimosaurids due to well-developed lower jaw musculature.
facts.quote: The length of the region where the lower jaw musculature attaches to is well developed and its length compared to that of the mandibular ramus indicates that Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis had a rather strong bite, easily comparable to some derived machimosaurids.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis had the highest posterior mechanical advantage among all known teleosaurs.
facts.quote: The posterior mechanical advantage (pMa) of I. potamosiamensis, which describes the overall maximum force along the toothrow, is the single highest among all teleosaurs.

facts.statement: Studies found that I. potamosiamensis had a high opening mechanical advantage for a strong bite, while I. kalasinensis had a low opening mechanical advantage allowing for a faster bite.
facts.quote: The study did find differences between I. potamosiamensis and the material at the time assigned to I. kalasinensis. The former was recovered as having an expectedly high opening mechanical advantage, the highest among teleosaurs, while the specimen attributed to I. kalasinensis had a relatively low oMa, giving it a much faster bite than.

facts.statement: There is a debate over whether differences between I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis represent distinct ecological niches or are due to post-mortem skull distortion.
facts.quote: This was initially interpreted as two contemporary species having filled different ecological niches, but other research has argued that the two forms were not distinst and that the differences were merely a matter of post-mortem distortion of the skull.

facts.statement: Researchers conclude that Indosinosuchus was likely a mesorostrine generalist without specific adaptations for hunting large or armored prey.
facts.quote: Although their precise ecology remains generally unresolved, Johnson and colleagues conclude that Indosinosuchus was most likely a mesorostrine generalist species, showing no particular adaptations for going after large or armored prey like derived machimosaurs.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis is one of the few confirmed purely freshwater teleosaurs.
facts.quote: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis is among the few known teleosaurs confirmed to have been purely freshwater animals, alongside an as of yet unnamed taxon from China.

facts.statement: The Phu Noi locality where I. potamosiamensis fossils were found represents an oxbow lake or abandoned river channel.
facts.quote: Specifically, the Phu Noi locality has been interpreted as representing an oxbow lake or the abandoned channel of one of the many meandering rivers of the region, given that the material was transported very little after the animal's deaths.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the age of the Phu Kradung Formation, with faunal evidence suggesting Late Jurassic and zircon/palynological data suggesting Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: To this come two contradictory hypothesis based on different methods. On the one hand, the general fauna of the formation better matches the Late Jurassic while dating using zircons and palynological data both point towards the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: A hypothesis suggests that freshwater teleosaurs were replaced by goniopholids and pholidosaurids in the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: This would be congruent with the hypothesis that freshwater teleosaurs, which were dominant in the lower parts of the formation were replaced by goniopholids and pholidosaurids such as Chalawan thailandicus during the Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Fossils of Indosinosuchus peninsularensis were found in a lagoonal environment with shallow peritidal conditions.
facts.quote: The part of the Khlong Min Formation that have yielded the fossils of Indosinosuchus peninsularensis on the other hand appears to represent a lagoonal environment with a closeby locality indicating shallow peritidal conditions above the fair weather wave base.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus peninsularensis was a coastal marine animal, unlike its freshwater relative I. potamosiamensis.
facts.quote: This means that rather than being a freshwater animal as its northern relative, Indosinosuchus peninsularensis was a coastal marine animal, a habitat preference more similar to other teleosauroids.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus peninsularensis dates to the late-Middle to early-Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: This species was furthermore older, dating to the late-Middle to early–Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: Ten Indosinosuchus specimens of varying ages were discovered at Phu Noi.
facts.quote: The discovery of 10 Indosinosuchus specimen at Phu Noi, which cover different ages from juvenile to full mature, raises the question how the animals of that particular assemblage died.

facts.statement: One hypothesis suggests a specimen was preserved after its bloated corpse floated on water, lost its head, and underwent rapid burial.
facts.quote: One specimen in particular, a nearly complete and still articulated vertebral column, could have been preserved when the bloated corpse of the animal floated on the water surface and lost its head, before undergoing rapid burial of the remaining body.

facts.statement: An alternative hypothesis proposes that the carcass was preserved by drying out rather than rapid burial.
facts.quote: Another hypothesis proposes that rather than rapid burial, it was the drying out of the carcass that caused its preservation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the Phu Noi specimens congregated in water during a major drought, a behavior seen in modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Martin and colleagues suggest that the Phu Noi Indosinosuchus specimen congregated in a body of water during a major drought, something still seen in modern species of crocodilians.

facts.statement: An alternative theory suggests the animals died in a flash flood and were stranded on dry land as waters receded.
facts.quote: Alternatively, the animals may have died in a flash flood, their decomposition beginning while the waters were still receding but eventually leaving the carcasses stranded on dry land.

facts.statement: The genus Indosinosuchus was described by Martin and colleagues in 2019.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Martin et al., 2019

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Indosinosuchus is Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis.
facts.quote: type_species: Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis

facts.statement: Two species are recognized within the genus: I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis.
facts.quote: subdivision: I. potamosiamensis Martin et al., 2019 I. kalasinensis Johnson, Young & Brusatte, 2020

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus is an extinct genus of teleosaurid crocodylomorph that lived in Thailand during the Jurassic.
facts.quote: Indosinosuchus es un género extinto de crocodilomorfo teleosáurido que vivió durante el Jurásico de Tailandia.

facts.statement: Indosinosuchus is the first confirmed case of a thalattosuchian that lived in freshwater habitats.
facts.quote: Indosinosuchus es el primer caso confirmado de un talatosuquio que vivió en hábitats de agua dulce.

facts.statement: While the horizon is thought to date to the Middle or Upper Jurassic, palynological data suggests it dates to the Early Cretaceous (Berriasian).
facts.quote: No es claro a qué época corresponde este horizonte, pero se piensa que data del Jurásico Medio o del Jurásico Superior. si bien los datos palinológicos sugieren que data del Cretácico Inferior (época del Berriasiense).

facts.statement: The species Indosinosuchus peninsularensis lived from the Bathonian to the Callovian, between 168.2 and 161.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Callovian (168.2 to 161.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: I. peninsularensis is diagnosed by features including the nasal reaching the 18th maxillary alveolus, lack of an incisive foramen, oval external nares, and broad ornamented osteoderms.
I. peninsularensis was discovered in a low-energy lagoonal environment, providing insights into teleosaurid ecology.
It is debated whether Asian teleosauroids occupied a broad spectrum of habitats, as evidenced by the contrast between fluvial and lagoonal/marine sediments.
